scope: the 12-bit id at bit 1309 OVERLAPS the count byte at 164 - which proves the bit position should be byte-aligned and the 1307 offset is a symptom of a mis-sized header

the_experiment.body: runs/snapshot-ent3.bin = ent2 + a 12-bit id (value 1) written at bit 1309
the_experiment.why_the_count_went_back_to_zero: the 12-bit id spans bits 1309..1320, which covers byte 163 bits 5-7 and ALL of byte 164 bits 0-7; writing id = 1 cleared byte 164 to 0x00, so the count byte was destroyed by the very field that follows it

the_arithmetic_that_exposes_the_problem.id_bits: 1309..1320 = byte 163 bits 5-7 + byte 164 bits 0-7 + byte 165 bit 0
the_arithmetic_that_exposes_the_problem.conclusion: the id region and the count byte OVERLAP by a full byte

what_that_proves: a format cannot have a byte-aligned whole-byte field inside a bit stream that continues over the same bytes
so the bit position at the entity block must be BYTE-ALIGNED in a real snapshot, i.e. a multiple of 8
1307 is not a multiple of 8, so a correct snapshot would reach the entity block at a byte boundary - which means OUR HEADER IS 5 BITS TOO LONG (or the preceding blocks are 5 bits short)

and that also explains why the count could be read at all in ent2: the count read used the BYTE cursor 164 while the bit cursor sat at 163.4, i.e. the two pointers were describing different places and the format was inconsistent
the_revised_target: make the bit position at the entity block equal to a multiple of 8 (ideally 1312 = byte 164)
then the gates would be bits 1312 and 1313, and the count byte would be byte 164 - read by the byte cursor AFTER the bit cursor has consumed exactly 2 bits from byte 164, i.e. consistent
the header is therefore 5 bits too long: shortening it by 5 bits (or moving the entity block 5 bits earlier) aligns everything
next: verify the hypothesis by building a body whose entity gates sit at a byte boundary: reduce the hybrid header from 1307 to 1304 or extend the ps/entity layout so that the entity block starts at 1312
the simplest test is to move the two gate bits to 1312/1313 and set the count byte at 164, keeping everything else, and see whether count = 1 AND the id reads back cleanly without overlap
